title: A density column: why liquids stack in layers
examples: Why does oil float on water?

layers.label: Honey

explain.say: Pour honey, washing-up liquid, water and cooking oil into a tall glass, gently. Wait a minute. They do not mix: they stack up in neat stripes! What decides the order? It is density, which means how much mass is packed into each bit of space.

explain.say: Between the washing-up liquid and the honey, brilliant! Solids follow the same rule: things less dense than a liquid float in it. Wow fact: the Dead Sea is so salty and dense that people float on it easily while reading a newspaper. Challenge: try your own column at home!

faq.q: Why does oil float on water?
faq.a: Oil is less dense than water, about 0.92 grams per cubic centimetre, so it rises and floats on top.
asks: Why don't oil and water mix?

faq.a: Density is how much mass is in each unit of volume. It is mass divided by volume, often in grams per cubic centimetre.

faq.q: Why does honey sink to the bottom?
faq.a: Honey is the densest liquid in the column, about 1.4 grams per cubic centimetre, so it sinks below the others.
Divide the mass by the volume. 200 grams of something with a volume of 100 cubic centimetres has a density of 2 grams per cubic centimetre.

faq.q: How do you know if something will float?
faq.a: If an object is less dense than the liquid, it floats. If it is denser, it sinks.

facts: Water has a density of about 1 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³).
